newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH METAL UNION WANTS BUFFER FUNDS TO BACK EMU.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH METAL UNION WANTS BUFFER FUNDS TO BACK EMU.

text.p: Finnish metal workers' union chairman Per-Erik Lundh said on Thursday that a tripartite agreement on buffer funds ensuring that unemployment benefits remain at current levels is a condition for the union to support Finnish EMU membership.
The metal workers' union is one of the most influential member unions of the 1.1-million member Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK).
The union led by Lundh represents 140,000 mainly blue-collar workers in metals, engineering and electrotechnical production. These sectors account for 40 percent of Finnish exports.
"Tripartite talks on the terms at which we join EMU should begin quickly," Lundh told the union council according to a copy of his prepared speech.

"The conditions set by us (SAK) are in many ways clear," he said, referring to recent SAK demands for significantly lower unemployment and so called buffer funds to cushion sharp cyclical downturns in exchange for union support for the social democrat-led government's bid to join EMU.
"We need various buffer funds," Lundh said, adding the most important one would be an unemployment security fund.

"Ensuring that this fund will maintain the level and duration of unemployment security benefits at least at the current level will be a central cornerstone of potential coming tripartite talks," he said.

Tripartite talks are held between central unions, employer confederations and the government. Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen recently signalled that the government was prepared to engage in such talks.
Employers have said they oppose any kind of buffer funds.
Lundh said he agreed with Lipponen's and Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto's view that a surplus of the state finances would be one of the best possible buffer funds.
"This can hardly be reached under the current timetable, or it would require such savings cures that would destroy other measures making EMU possible," he said.

Lipponen's five-party left-right-green government has repeatedly said its aim is for Finland to be in the first group of countries joining the planned third stage of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union.
Trade union support is regarded as vital to swing Lipponen's own social democratic parliamentary group behind EMU.
Lundh said nobody knew what kind of economic and fiscal policy scenario would face the countries establishing EMU.
"It is clear that at least national buffer funds must be set up to take care of cyclical swings and crises if the common currency ... is implemented without a common EU budget," he said.
Companies could set up their own buffer funds, he said, adding so called holiday pay, the 13th month salary, could provide some room to manoeuver.

Lundh also said Finland's system of centralised colective bargaining talks should be maintained also if Finland joined EMU. "Our economy is so small that it is useless to join EMU and face potential cyclical swings without this kind of united and unifying system," he said.
Lundh reiterated the trade unions' strong opposition to employer calls for nominal wage flexibility in EMU.

"The price and availability of energy, the price and availability of raw material and the price of capital are production components with far more impact on total output and our competitiveness," he said.
"The best preparation for EMU is that we really start to improve employment," Lundh said.
It was also important to work determinedly towards raising the degree of refinement of Finnish production.
"By raising the degree of refinement we prevent that Finland would become a low-wage area," he said.
